subject: Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?

messages.author: 81e473ecfda78ff0
messages.subject: Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?
parts:
Dear List,

We conducted an aerial line transect survey with two observers (left/right side of the aircraft). A hazard-rate detection function with observer as factor covariate was selected by AIC as an appropriate detection function (both observers had high detection near the line, but one observer detected fewer animals in the distance ‘bin’ furthest away from the track-line.

I would appreciate your input to better understand the implications of having a detection function with observer as a covariate for DSM modelling. Particularly whether (or why) this is a negative outcome relative to the situation where both left and right observers had the same detection function. I’ll try to answer some of this myself, but appreciate your corrections and additions to the statements below.

One negative aspect is that observer change within segments and therefore we cannot use a count model for DSM, or dsm.var.prop for variance propagation.  

But what about estimates of density in the DSM? Are these prone to bias because we have ‘observer effect’ present in the detection function? Instead of observed counts, we now use a Horvitz-Thompson-like estimate of abundance per segment in the DSM. This takes into account the detection probability (p), which in our case is the average probability of detection from both observers (?)  

Thanks in advance for any comments.

Chris

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?
parts:
Chris

I won't claim to have all the insights regarding the consequences of observer effects in detectability upon density surface model results; I can't think my way through all of the implications.

But recognise there are many other unmodelled covariates that are affecting the detection function (you know the list: glare, sea state, what the observers had for lunch, ...)  Conventional distance sampling enjoys the benefits of pooling robustness that says the estimates are unbiased even when these myriad covariates are not modelled.

Because of pooling robustness, I would rank the exclusion of an observer effect high on the "difficulties with my analysis" list.  Perhaps I am overlooking something; and others on the list will correct my assertion.

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?
parts:
Chris, if both observers are operating simultaneously, one either side, then there is no problem.  As Eric notes, pooling robustness means all is OK.  If you had segments where one observer only is used, then segments where the other observer only operated, there probably wouldn’t be an issue if these segments alternated and were short – too short to affect the density surface model.  If the segments were long, then you might start to see an effect if you did relatively little smoothing in the DSM, especially at or near the edges of the study area.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?
parts:
Thank you very much Eric and Stephen for your answers. Sounds like good news, overall. 
Perhaps it is also useful for someone looking at this post in future to link to a recent paper I just came across that deals with uncertainty in the detection probability and propagating this uncertainty (regardless of detection function complexity) to DSM models (a potential issue I mentioned in my original post).

Bravington, M.V., Miller, D.L. & Hedley, S.L. Variance Propagation for Density Surface Models. JABES (2021). https://doi.org/10.1007/s13253-021-00438-2

Chris

parts:
Hi Chris,

Yes, that paper is cited at the bottom of the help page for dsm.var.prop
(at least in dsm version 2.3.1, which was release at the end of last month).

In case it's helpful, there are lots of tips on fitting density surface
models, focussed on marine mammal data but useful in other contexts, at

https://osf.io/yp27g/wiki/home/

I didn't see any explicit mention of implications of using
observer-level covariates there, but if you think it would be useful to
add anything you could drop a line to the wiki maintainer, Jason Roberts
(listed under "contact us") on that page.

Good luck with your analyses, Len Thomas
